note.text: In the traditional school account, simple apprehension forms or grasps a concept without yet affirming or denying anything. Judgment affirms or denies a relation and is expressed in a proposition. Reasoning connects judgments so that one is supported by others. A term expresses a concept; a proposition can be true or false; an argument contains an inference. These operations are linked but are not interchangeable. Thinking of market alone does not assert that a market is open.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: In the traditional school account, simple apprehension forms or grasps a concept without yet affirming or denying anything. Judgment affirms or denies a relation and is expressed in a proposition. Reasoning connects judgments so that one is supported by others. A term expresses a concept; a proposition can be true or false; an argument contains an inference. These operations are linked but are not interchangeable. Thinking of market alone does not assert that a market is open.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Ngozi thinks about a market: she grasps an idea. She then judges that the market is open today. Finally she reasons that traders can enter because the market is open and entry is permitted. The last move needs premises and a conclusion. Each stage adds a different logical role, rather than simply a longer phrase.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask whether the example merely names something, asserts something or supports a claim from other claims. Do not classify every sentence as reasoning: a bare assertion gives no supporting inference. The traditional terminology is the course framework, not a claim that psychologists classify every thought this way.
